Read `README.md` and current rollout evidence first. Produce exactly one multi-wake target-policy candidate in `solver/`. Keep candidate-specific reasoning in `logs/optimize/wake_policy_notes.md`, and add or materially revise at least one evidence-backed reusable lesson in `guidance/control_experience.md` from the assigned parent, sampled solver results, and inherited logs. If no positive lesson survives the evidence, record a concrete negative result and what later workers should avoid or test. The candidate is incomplete until both files are updated. Work only inside this Phase 2 workspace.

Use the fish-control bookshelf through this structured transfer protocol:

1. Before the first architecture proposal from the common naive seed, consult `guidance/skills/fish-control-primitives/SKILL.md` and its references.
2. On later iterations, consult it again when the inherited guidance indicates three consecutive completed iterations with neither a new controller mechanism nor a semantic improvement such as a new success, a better termination class, or a meaningfully different useful trajectory.
3. Consultation is required at those moments; adopting a primitive is optional. Do not use the shelf to justify scalar-only gain tuning.
4. If a source informs the edit, record a concise block in `logs/optimize/wake_policy_notes.md`:

```text
bookshelf_consulted: true
source_domain:
source_mechanism:
transferable_invariant:
nontransferable_details:
policy_translation:
falsification:
```

Translate only the invariant into normalized body-frame observations and the two-joint state-feedback contract. Prefer one mechanism or one small compatible combination. Published gains, species-specific kinematics, exact vortex phases, and task-specific routes are not transferable answers.

I’ll start with the workspace contract and inherited rollout evidence, then inspect both wake visualizations before proposing the single candidate. I’m using the fish-control bookshelf because you explicitly required its transfer protocol, and the wake-visual skill because policy edits here must be grounded in both 3D moving-window views.

The workspace is a later prefilled iteration, but the shelf consultation is still required by your instruction. I’m now comparing all four sampled rollouts—including metrics, diagnostics, inherited notes, and the best finite versus most informative failure images—before writing the pre-edit diagnosis.

The evidence now isolates the gap: the inherited velocity-course controller is the only mechanism with a sub‑1L pass, but three terminal overlays (`0.838–0.867L`) all preserve the same left-exit topology. At closest approach the request remains saturated and the fish is still moving about `0.79–0.85U`; static curvature, an anterior center shift, and one-sided posterior relief do not supply corrective yaw. I’m checking the sibling inherited lessons to avoid repeating another already-falsified terminal mechanism.

The bookshelf transfer is informing one compact mechanism: retain slow body-frame target-course steering, but replace the failed joint-angle proxy with a bounded, terminal-only residual keyed to the measured yaw moment itself. This tests whether suppressing only observed counter-turn moment can add the missing impulse without another static bend, route, timer, or global gain escalation. I’m recording that pre-edit hypothesis now, as required.

The pre-edit provenance note is now in place. The single policy edit will preserve the validated velocity-course carrier and add only a bounded, terminal, measured-yaw-moment residual; this replaces the failed anterior-angle proxy with the load signal the rollout actually measured.

The candidate and durable guidance lesson are both updated. A trace replay confirms the new residual is exactly zero outside `3.5L`, is active on about 10% of the inherited trajectory, and is bounded at `4 rad/T²`; it reaches full authority only during the measured counter-moment portion of the tangent pass. I’m invoking the required contract checker now—no CFD will be run.

The configured checker could not start because its pinned `gpt-5.4-mini` model is unavailable on this account. I’m applying the same three commands from its immutable TOML locally, separately, and will repair and rerun any failure.

The first checker found a rendered-workspace defect: `README.md` contains the identical assigned-parent marker twice, so it cannot identify “exactly one” parent even though both point to the same optimizer. I’m removing only that duplicate administrative entry, then rerunning the required check unchanged.

The guidance check now passes. The Julia contract command is blocked by the environment—not by the candidate: the configured shell has no `julia` executable. I’m locating any bundled Julia runtime before treating that check as unavailable; the schema and boundary checks can still run deterministically.

The Julia contract command is blocked by the environment rather than the candidate: no `julia` executable is on PATH (the login shell also emitted unrelated missing-SSH-home setup warnings). I’m checking the workspace and standard installation roots for the evaluator’s Julia binary; if absent, I’ll still complete the deterministic schema/static checks and report the environmental limitation precisely.

Completed the single candidate:

- [candidate_target_policy.jl](solver/cases/dogfish_3d_shape_policy/candidate_target_policy.jl:1): terminal measured-yaw-moment rejection added to the inherited velocity-course carrier.
- [wake_policy_notes.md](logs/optimize/wake_policy_notes.md:1): visual diagnosis, hypothesis, falsification criteria, and bookshelf transfer block.
- [control_experience.md](guidance/control_experience.md:118): reusable negative lesson covering the three failed terminal-authority approaches.

Guidance and boundary checks pass, as does the static parameter-schema guard. The configured checker was invoked but its pinned model was unavailable; the Julia runtime check also could not execute because Julia is not installed. No CFD was run.
